newsitem.title: USA: Cash crudes drive higher in U.S. trade, LLS gains.
newsitem.headline: Cash crudes drive higher in U.S. trade, LLS gains.

text.p: U.S. cash crude prices worked higher late Thursday afternoon, aided by nervous buying on the potential for a longer-than-expected hiatus for Iraqi crude sales under the renewed "oil-for-food" accord.

Even though Iraq received permission last week to sell another $2.14 billion worth of crude oil from June 8 for 180 days, Baghdad has not submitted a pricing formula for new oil contracts. Iraq said it would wait until the U.N. approved an aid distribution plan before handing over a pricing scheme, effectively stalling oil liftings until at least end-June when the aid plan should be complete.

Trade sources said talk of more lengthy delays for resumed Iraqi exports bolstered outright crude prices on thoughts 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of exports would be out of circulation until mid-July.

There was, however, no report of a change in Iraqi policy that it was not delaying the oil sales for any political reason. On Wednesday, Iraqi Ambassador to the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, said the delays in oil lifting were not irregular and were part of working out new procedures.
July NYMEX futures settled at $18.69 a barrel, 16 cents higher than Wednesday, but late afternoon ACCESS trade pushed the market another 16 cents higher to $18.85 a barrel.

The futures market buying allowed cash benchmark July West Texas Intermediate/Cushing to talk late in the session at $18.95-19.05, figuring in a 15-16 cents premium from the current Exchange for Physicals rate. Late benchmark crude was about 25 cents higher from prices pegged on Wednesday.
"There were no sellers (late U.S. trade) in the market. People were talking about these cash market rumors that Iraqi oil might not be coming until mid-July," said a trader.

For the grades, Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James sold late at a 14 cents discount to the WTI/Cushing benchmark, three cents weaker than the strongest deals of the session at marker -11 cents. Still, late LLS values were some seven cents higher than Wednesday. Traders said a combination of refiner buying and short covering plays related to unsold foreign cargoes, aided the uptick.
"Short covering, storage plays and renewed refiner interest all helped the Louisiana sweets," said a trader.
Sour crudes were stuck around a $1.60-63 discount for West Texas Sour/Midland, and at a steady $2.05 discount for Eugene Island barrels. July WTI/Cushing Postings hung around deals at $1.80-83.
